details:
**Child with Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park**
Diane Arbus's 1962 photograph of a skinny boy (Colin Wood) with one strap of his overalls falling off his shoulder, clutching a toy grenade and making a manic grimace. Arbus, known for her square-format black-and-white portraits of outsiders such as the "Jewish Giant," worked mostly in New York.

**V-J Day in Times Square**
Alfred Eisenstaedt's 1945 Life photograph of a sailor bending back and kissing a woman in a white dress in Times Square, during the celebrations of Japan's surrender at the end of World War II.

**Lunch Atop a Skyscraper**
A staged 1932 photograph of eleven construction workers eating lunch on a steel girder hundreds of feet above Manhattan during construction of the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center. It is usually credited to Charles Ebbets and is among the best-selling stock images ever.

**Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives**
Riis's 1890 photojournalism book exposing the squalor of New York's Lower East Side tenements, whose title comes from a line in Rabelais' Pantagruel. Its photos include Bandit's Roost, showing a gang in a Mulberry Street alley, with a man in a bowler hat and a woman leaning out of a window.

**Paul Strand's Wall Street**
Strand's 1915 photograph of tiny pedestrians casting long shadows as they walk past the huge, dark, rectangular windows of the J. P. Morgan bank building. It is a landmark of "straight photography," along with work by Alfred Stieglitz, whose 291 gallery was in New York.

**Chrysler Building**
William Van Alen's Art Deco skyscraper (1930), built for the Chrysler car company. Its stainless-steel crown of terraced arches is adorned with eagle-head gargoyles and ornaments shaped like car radiator caps; it is the world's tallest brick building.

**Central Park**
The Manhattan park designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux. It contains the statue of the sled dog Balto, an Egyptian obelisk called Cleopatra's Needle (others are in London and Paris), the Angel of the Waters atop Bethesda Fountain, and Belvedere Castle; in 2005 Christo and Jeanne-Claude installed The Gates, 7,503 saffron fabric gates, along its paths. Charles Ives depicted it in Central Park in the Dark.

**Patience and Fortitude**
The two marble lions guarding the entrance of the New York Public Library's main branch on Fifth Avenue beside Bryant Park. Mayor Fiorello La Guardia gave them these names during the Great Depression.

**Charging Bull and Fearless Girl**
Arturo Di Modica's bronze Charging Bull stands near Wall Street and the New York Stock Exchange in the Financial District. In 2017, Kristen Visbal's statue Fearless Girl was installed facing it; it was later moved to stand opposite the Stock Exchange.

**Statue of Liberty and "The New Colossus"**
Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi's copper statue in New York Harbor, a gift from France, showing a crowned woman holding a torch with broken chains at her feet; it has turned green from oxidation. Emma Lazarus's sonnet "The New Colossus" ("Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses") is on a plaque at its base.

**Basquiat, Keith Haring, and Andy Warhol**
New York's 1980s downtown art scene centered on the East Village and SoHo. Jean-Michel Basquiat first wrote graffiti as SAMO© with Al Diaz (ending with "SAMO© IS DEAD") and used a three-pointed crown motif; Keith Haring, known for his "radiant baby," painted the mural Crack Is Wack. Andy Warhol produced his silkscreens of Marilyn Monroe at his Manhattan studio, The Factory.

**One World Trade Center and Falling Man**
One World Trade Center (the "Freedom Tower"), from a master plan by Daniel Libeskind, rises a symbolic 1,776 feet at the site of the Twin Towers destroyed on September 11, 2001; the annual Tribute in Light uses 88 vertical searchlights. Richard Drew's photo The Falling Man shows a man falling headfirst from the North Tower against its vertical lines.

**Museums: MoMA, the Met, and the Whitney**
The Museum of Modern Art (first directed by Alfred H. Barr Jr.) holds van Gogh's The Starry Night, Henri Rousseau's The Sleeping Gypsy, and Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans. The Metropolitan Museum of Art on the "Museum Mile" holds El Greco's View of Toledo, and the Whitney beside the High Line holds Ben Shahn's The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti.

**Films set in New York**
Martin Scorsese's Taxi Driver features Robert De Niro as Travis Bickle ("You talkin' to me?"), and The Godfather depicts the Corleone crime family. Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing is set on a Brooklyn block with Sal's pizzeria and Radio Raheem, and other films include Birdman, The Wolf of Wall Street, and Synecdoche, New York.

**Dance in New York**
The Lindy Hop flourished at Harlem's Savoy Ballroom (Frankie Manning, Whitey's Lindy Hoppers), breakdancing arose in the Bronx to DJ Kool Herc's drum breaks, and voguing emerged from the ballroom scene shown in Paris Is Burning. The city is home to George Balanchine's New York City Ballet, American Ballet Theatre (where Misty Copeland became the first Black female principal dancer in 2015), and the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, known for Revelations.
